one_liner: Embeddable transactional LSM key-value engine in C; the author's benchmark shows 4-5x RocksDB's iterator-seek throughput at about 3.5x the memory.
what_it_does: TidesDB is a persistent LSM-tree storage engine library in C that you build a database on or embed as a key-value/column-family store. It has its own C API, not RocksDB's: tidesdb_open with a config struct, column families, and every get/put/delete/iterator running inside a tidesdb_txn_* transaction. Transactions are MVCC with 5 isolation levels (read-uncommitted through serializable) and 2PC-XA. It also offers bidirectional range-bounded iterators, range deletes, TTL and optional Snappy/LZ4/Zstd encoding.
how_it_is_fast: The benchmarked v6.1.0 kept SSTable metadata resident until it was provably safe to free: sparse block indices, per-SSTable bloom filters (~10 bits/key), min/max keys and open file handles. Its partitioned CLOCK block cache (2 shards per core, lock-free hits, atomic refcounts) held already-deserialized key-log blocks, so a seek to hot data needed no syscall, decompression or parsing. The current v10 line changes the structure. Each SSTable's key log is a B+tree whose parsed nodes are cached and whose root stays pinned, whole-file blooms are replaced by partitioned range filters, and WiscKey-style key/value separation keeps values of 1 KiB and up out of the tree, which shortens it. Compaction follows Spooky (partitioned merges on the largest level's boundaries, Dynamic Capacity Adaptation).
when_to_use: Seek-heavy or point-lookup-heavy workloads over small keys and values (16 B / 100 B in the benchmark) with a hot working set that fits in RAM: iterator Seek ran 4.2x (random), 4.7x (sequential) and 5.3x (Zipfian) faster than RocksDB 10.7.5 at 8 threads.
Short range scans (about 100 keys) where positioning the iterator dominates the cost (2.41x faster than RocksDB at 100 random keys).

Write-heavy ingest of values of 1 KiB and up where key/value separation pays: the author's v10.0.0 vs RocksDB 11.8.1 defaults run reports 2-10x faster seeding of a 10 GiB dataset and 2.5-5.4x lower write amplification.
Embedded C/C++ services that want multi-column-family atomic transactions, MVCC snapshots, isolation levels up to serializable and XA two-phase commit in one library with no mandatory dependencies.
Slow SATA-class storage under default RocksDB settings, where RocksDB's L0 write stalls dominate (the author's small-server median advantage was 3.8x, against 1.82x on NVMe).
when_not_to_use: Memory-constrained deployments (containers with ~2 GB limits, many instances per host). Peak RSS was 851 MB vs RocksDB's 246 MB in the seek benchmark, and 2.4-4.4x RocksDB's raw peak on three of four v10 keybench workloads. Filter directories are held outside the block-cache budget.

Long range scans that need values. 1000-key ranges were a tie (1.11x, within variance per the author), there is no parallel value-log prefetch, and every separated value costs an extra read per entry.
When you need RocksDB API compatibility, its tooling and ecosystem, or custom comparators. v10 removed comparators, so keys must be encoded to sort correctly by memcmp.

When you need a stable on-disk format or a long-proven engine. Four major versions shipped between Dec 2025 (v6.1.0) and Sep 2026 (v10.0.0); 10.x cannot read 9.x files and migration is dump-and-reload. About 97% of commits come from one maintainer.
Tight disk budgets. In the v10 keybench the store averaged about 2x its live data because of value-log retention, and the author says to size disks for the peak.

integration.form: shared lib (static by default on Windows); CMake package TidesDB::tidesdb, public header <tidesdb/db.h>
integration.dependencies: none mandatory (C standard library + threads; xxHash bundled); optional Snappy, LZ4, Zstd, and optionally mimalloc/tcmalloc/jemalloc
integration.min_toolchain: C11 with atomics; CMake 3.12+; GCC 7+, Clang 6+, MSVC 2019 16.8+ (/experimental:c11atomics)
integration.platforms: Linux (x86, x64, ARM64, PowerPC32, RISC-V64), macOS (x64, Apple Silicon), Windows (x86/x64, MSVC and MinGW), FreeBSD/OpenBSD/NetBSD/DragonFlyBSD/Illumos/Solaris x64; 32-bit and PowerPC targets need libatomic
integration.thread_safety: The tidesdb_t handle is thread-safe and meant to be shared by every thread. Transaction handles are not thread-safe (one thread per transaction; only tidesdb_txn_request_abort may cross threads). A directory can be opened by only one handle at a time, enforced by an OFD/flock/LockFileEx lock.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — different C API (transaction-scoped get/put/iterators, column families), no RocksDB API shim, and incompatible file formats

gotchas: Durability is off by default (memtable_sync_mode = TDB_SYNC_NONE). Set TDB_SYNC_FULL or TDB_SYNC_INTERVAL if acknowledged commits must survive a crash. The headline benchmark also ran with sync disabled on both engines.

TDB_ERR_LOCKED from a read means a source was busy (memtable rotation, file-descriptor budget exhausted) and you must retry. The docs call treating it as not-found a correctness bug. TDB_ERR_CONFLICT likewise needs a retry loop.
Buffers the library returns must be freed with tidesdb_free, never free(). With a non-default allocator build, calling free() crashes.

The benchmarked seek path belongs to an architecture that no longer exists (block-format key logs, whole-file bloom filters). An iterator-seek correctness bug (issue #490: seek returned too few keys after reopen, due to a wrong early exit) was found against v7.0.2 and fixed in Dec 2025, so re-benchmark your own workload on v10.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TidesDB over TerarkDB (a RocksDB 5.18 fork that is drop-in for RocksDB) when you can adopt a new C API and want an actively maintained engine with MVCC transactions and key/value separation. Pick it over libmdbx or redb (B-tree engines) for write-heavy or large-value ingest and multi-column-family LSM workloads, accepting more RAM and format churn. Bourbon is a research artifact, not a library you would ship.
verified_claims_summary: The TidesDB author's Dec 2025 benchtool run compared TidesDB v6.1.0 with RocksDB v10.7.5, both C libraries built with GCC -O3, on an i7-11700K with 48 GB RAM and a SATA SSD under Ubuntu 23.04: 8 threads, 16 B keys / 100 B values, no fsync. It measured iterator Seek() on 5M keys at 3.73M vs 893K ops/s random (4.17x), 8.87M vs 1.87M sequential (4.74x) and 3.56M vs 679K Zipfian (5.25x); 100-key scans were 2.41x faster and 1000-key scans 1.11x (a tie). Caveats: this is a first-party vendor result, the article's own conclusion quotes different figures (4.11x/4.58x/6.31x), and no C++ std baseline is involved.
status_note: Very active (v10.0.2 released 2026-09-24, pushed 2026-09-26) and MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft, fine to link from proprietary code), but effectively a one-maintainer project that breaks its on-disk format at each major release; the v6.1.0 design the headline numbers come from has since been replaced.
